title: Streamline benchmark artifact pipeline for model onboarding profiles
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Problem: The current benchmark harness produces performance profiles that are inconsistent across runs, lack standardized metadata, and are produced by a mix of ad-hoc eval runners. This makes it hard to reliably publish model performance artifacts for onboarding and for the runtime to select compatible model variants.

Goal: Improve the benchmark harness so it reliably generates complete, machine-readable performance profiles for new model versions. Profiles should include: model_version, quantization/config, kernel hints, hardware target, batch/seq distribution, latency/throughput percentiles, compute cost estimate (tokens/sec and inferred $/1M tokens), and quality metrics for the supplied datasets/prompts. Profiles must be reproducible, signed (artifact integrity), and stored in the canonical artifact store.

Scope:
- Replace several bespoke eval scripts with a single pluggable harness that runs task-specific eval runners (generation, classification, embeddings, reranking).
- Standardize datasets and prompt templates via a dataset registry (manifest + sampled subsets) and canonical prompt schema (metadata, instruction, examples, expected_output_type).
- Record deterministic seeds and environment metadata (OS, docker image, commit hash, compiled kernels) so profiles are comparable across hardware and runtime versions.
- Add multi-mode runs: "full" (comprehensive metrics, slow), "smoke" (fast subset for PR gating), and "sampled" (statistically representative for periodic jobs).
- Output compact JSON profile artifacts and optional CSV/time-series outputs for visualization.

Design decisions / trade-offs considered:
- Determinism vs representativeness: to keep run durations reasonable we will use stratified sampling for long datasets and persist sampling seeds in the manifest. Full runs remain available as a separate pipeline.
- Runner language: Python harness (pytest-compatible runners) to reuse existing eval code, but workers will be spawnable via a lightweight Go worker when low overhead is needed. For now prioritize Python for developer velocity.
- Storage and signing: profiles written to s3://redwood-inference-benchmarks/{model}/{version}/profile.json and signed using the existing KMS signing key. This adds small latency but improves artifact integrity.

Acceptance criteria:
- New harness runs a full onboarding job end-to-end and produces a profile.json with the required fields documented above.
- Profiles include at minimum: latency P50/P90/P95/P99, tokens/sec, estimated $/1M tokens, dataset coverage, seed, runtime commit, and kernel hints.
- PR gating uses smoke mode (<=10% samples) and fails on regression in latency (>10% P90) or quality (task-specific thresholds).
- Generated profiles are uploaded and accessible in the artifact store, and a sample profile is linked from the model onboarding page.
- Unit tests for the harness and an integration test in CI that runs smoke mode on a small model.

Risks:
- Long full-run compute cost. Mitigation: enforce quotas, cache intermediate outputs, and only run full on release or triggered pipelines.
- Different hardware leads to divergent kernels; we must tag profiles by hardware and allow runtime mapping rules.

Next steps:
1) Merge initial harness skeleton and dataset registry PR (WIP).
2) Implement smoke-mode CI gating and threshold config.
3) Add artifact signing and storage integration.
4) Documentation for PMs and Onboarding/IR teams on how to interpret the profile.
